subject: Physics
topic: 1.0 General Physics — Physical Quantities, Units, Measurement, Data, Vectors and Uncertainties
content:
ZIMSEC / MoPSE 2024–2030 SCOPE
This topic establishes the measurement, mathematical and data-handling language used throughout Advanced Level Physics. The revised Zimbabwe Forms 5–6 syllabus places Physical Quantities and Units and Errors and Uncertainties under General Physics. Students are expected to use SI units, derive units, test equations for homogeneity, present data correctly, manipulate vectors, distinguish accuracy from precision, combine uncertainties and interpret graphs.

1.1 PHYSICAL QUANTITIES
A physical quantity is a measurable property expressed as a numerical value together with a unit. Examples include length, mass, time, temperature, electric current, amount of substance and luminous intensity. A measurement without an appropriate unit is incomplete.

A scalar has magnitude only. Examples: mass, time, temperature, energy, speed, distance and density.
A vector has both magnitude and direction. Examples: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum and electric field strength.

SI BASE QUANTITIES
Length: metre (m)
Mass: kilogram (kg)
Time: second (s)
Electric current: ampere (A)
Thermodynamic temperature: kelvin (K)
Amount of substance: mole (mol)
Luminous intensity: candela (cd)

Common derived quantities:
Area: m²
Volume: m³
Speed/velocity: m s⁻¹
Acceleration: m s⁻²
Force: newton, N = kg m s⁻²
Energy/work: joule, J = kg m² s⁻²
Power: watt, W = kg m² s⁻³
Pressure: pascal, Pa = kg m⁻¹ s⁻²
Charge: coulomb, C = A s
Potential difference: volt, V = kg m² s⁻³ A⁻¹
Resistance: ohm, Ω = kg m² s⁻³ A⁻²
Capacitance: farad, F = kg⁻¹ m⁻² s⁴ A²
Magnetic flux density: tesla, T = kg s⁻² A⁻¹

PREFIXES
pico p = 10⁻¹²
nano n = 10⁻⁹
micro μ = 10⁻⁶
milli m = 10⁻³
centi c = 10⁻²
deci d = 10⁻¹
kilo k = 10³
mega M = 10⁶
giga G = 10⁹
tera T = 10¹²

Students must be careful with symbols: m means milli only when used as a prefix, while m is also the SI symbol for metre; M means mega and must not be confused with m.

1.2 DIMENSIONAL ANALYSIS AND HOMOGENEITY
A physical equation is homogeneous when both sides have the same dimensions. Dimensional analysis is useful for checking equations and deriving relationships.

Dimensions are represented using base symbols such as [M] for mass, [L] for length and [T] for time.
Velocity: [LT⁻¹]
Acceleration: [LT⁻²]
Force: [MLT⁻²]
Energy: [ML²T⁻²]
Power: [ML²T⁻³]
Pressure: [ML⁻¹T⁻²]

Example:
For v² = u² + 2as:
[v²] = L²T⁻².
[u²] = L²T⁻².
[as] = (LT⁻²)(L) = L²T⁻².
Therefore the equation is dimensionally homogeneous.

Dimensional analysis cannot by itself establish numerical dimensionless constants such as 2, π or 1/2. It also cannot prove that an equation is physically correct merely because it is dimensionally correct.

1.3 DATA PRESENTATION
Tables must have clear headings, units and consistent decimal places where appropriate. Do not repeat units unnecessarily in every cell if the unit is already stated in the column heading. Graph axes require labels and units. Independent variables are normally plotted on the horizontal axis and dependent variables on the vertical axis.

A good graph:
• uses a sensible scale occupying a large portion of the plotting area;
• labels both axes with quantity and unit;
• plots points accurately;
• uses a smooth curve or a best-fit straight line as appropriate;
• avoids joining experimental points dot-to-dot unless the situation requires it;
• includes an appropriate origin when justified;
• identifies anomalous points;
• allows a gradient or intercept to be determined.

Gradient:
gradient = change in y / change in x.
For a straight-line relationship y = mx + c, m is the gradient and c is the y-intercept.

The area under a graph can represent a physical quantity. Examples:
• area under a velocity-time graph = displacement;
• area under a force-time graph = impulse;
• area under a pressure-volume graph = work done by a gas when the appropriate path and sign convention are used.

1.4 VECTORS
A vector should be represented by an arrow. Arrow length represents magnitude and arrow direction represents direction. Vector addition follows the triangle or parallelogram method.

For two perpendicular components:
Ax = A cos θ
Ay = A sin θ
where θ is measured from the positive x-axis.

Magnitude:
A = √(Ax² + Ay²)

Direction:
tan θ = Ay/Ax
The quadrant must be considered when reporting the direction.

For two vectors A and B with angle θ between them:
R = √(A² + B² + 2AB cos θ)

For components:
Rx = Σx-components
Ry = Σy-components
R = √(Rx² + Ry²)

Equilibrium of a particle requires the vector sum of all forces to be zero:
ΣFx = 0
ΣFy = 0.

Students should distinguish between adding magnitudes and adding vectors. Two forces of 5 N each do not necessarily produce 10 N; the result depends on their relative directions.

1.5 MEASUREMENT
In practical work, the measured value depends on the instrument and method. Resolution is the smallest scale division or smallest change that can normally be distinguished. A digital instrument may display a fixed number of decimal places, but displayed digits do not automatically guarantee equivalent accuracy.

For repeated measurements, calculate a mean where appropriate:
mean = sum of measurements / number of measurements.

An anomalous result is one that does not fit the general pattern of the repeated measurements. It should not simply be deleted without justification. Investigate possible experimental causes.

1.6 ERRORS AND UNCERTAINTIES
The syllabus requires students to distinguish systematic and random errors and accuracy and precision, and to estimate uncertainty in derived quantities by addition of actual, fractional or percentage uncertainties.

Systematic error shifts measurements consistently in one direction. Examples include zero error, a wrongly calibrated instrument and a consistent parallax problem. Repeating the measurement usually does not remove a systematic error.

Random error varies unpredictably between measurements. Repeated measurements and averaging can reduce the effect of random error.

Accuracy describes closeness to the accepted or true value.
Precision describes the closeness of repeated measurements to one another.

A set of readings can be precise but inaccurate if a systematic error is present.

Absolute uncertainty:
A measurement may be written x ± Δx.

Fractional uncertainty:
Δx/x

Percentage uncertainty:
(Δx/x) × 100%.

For addition or subtraction of quantities, absolute uncertainties are normally combined:
z = x + y
Δz = Δx + Δy.

For multiplication or division, fractional or percentage uncertainties are combined:
z = xy
Δz/z ≈ Δx/x + Δy/y.

For powers:
z = xⁿ
fractional uncertainty in z ≈ |n| times fractional uncertainty in x.

Example:
If r = (2.00 ± 0.01) m, then the percentage uncertainty in r is 0.5%. For A = πr², the percentage uncertainty is approximately 1.0%.

1.7 UNCERTAINTY IN GRAPHS
Error bars represent uncertainty in measured values. A line of best fit should represent the overall trend rather than pass through every point.

A worst acceptable line is a line that is still reasonably consistent with the error bars but has an extreme gradient. The uncertainty in gradient can be estimated from:
absolute uncertainty in gradient ≈ |gradient of best fit − gradient of worst acceptable line|.

The same principle can be used for the y-intercept.

Always give final experimental values as:
quantity = value ± uncertainty unit.

1.8 SIGNIFICANT FIGURES AND ROUNDING
Do not report a result with unjustified precision. The number of significant figures should reflect the measurements and uncertainties. Keep extra digits during intermediate calculations and round the final answer.

Scientific notation is useful for very large and very small values:
3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

1.9 PRACTICAL CHECKLIST
Before recording data:
• identify the independent and dependent variables;
• identify control variables;
• choose an appropriate instrument;
• consider zero errors and calibration;
• plan repeated readings;
• identify safety hazards.

During an experiment:
• record raw readings immediately;
• use consistent units;
• record uncertainty;
• avoid parallax;
• repeat readings where appropriate;
• do not fabricate or silently alter anomalous data.

For analysis:
• calculate derived quantities;
• plot an appropriate graph;
• determine gradient/intercept when required;
• estimate uncertainty;
• compare with theory;
• discuss limitations and improvements.

1.10 EXAM-STYLE REASONING
When asked to “define”, give a precise formal definition.
When asked to “state”, give a concise answer.
When asked to “explain”, include the physical reasoning.
When asked to “describe”, give the relevant sequence or features.
When asked to “compare”, give similarities and differences.
When asked to “deduce”, show how the supplied information leads to the result.
When asked to “suggest”, give a physically reasonable method or explanation.

CORE FORMULAE
v = Δs/Δt
a = Δv/Δt
F = ma
p = mv
W = Fs
P = W/t
ρ = m/V

1.11 WORKED EXAMPLE: UNIT DERIVATION
Suppose pressure is defined as force divided by area.
Force has unit N = kg m s⁻².
Area has unit m².
Therefore:
pressure = N/m² = kg m s⁻²/m² = kg m⁻¹ s⁻².
This is the pascal.

1.12 WORKED EXAMPLE: DIMENSIONAL CHECK
Check v = √(2gh).
The dimensions of gh are:
(LT⁻²)(L) = L²T⁻².
The square root gives LT⁻¹, which is the dimension of velocity. The equation is therefore dimensionally homogeneous.

1.13 WORKED EXAMPLE: VECTOR RESOLUTION
A force of 80 N acts at 30° above the horizontal.
Horizontal component:
Fx = 80 cos30° ≈ 69.3 N.
Vertical component:
Fy = 80 sin30° = 40.0 N.
If another force acts horizontally in the opposite direction, the horizontal component can be balanced independently of the vertical component.

1.14 WORKED EXAMPLE: RESULTANT OF PERPENDICULAR VECTORS
A displacement has components 12 m east and 5 m north.
Magnitude:
R = √(12² + 5²) = 13 m.
Direction:
θ = tan⁻¹(5/12) ≈ 22.6° north of east.

1.15 WORKED EXAMPLE: UNCERTAINTY
Length L = 50.0 ± 0.5 cm.
Percentage uncertainty = 0.5/50.0 × 100 = 1.0%.
If area A = L², percentage uncertainty in A ≈ 2.0%.
The uncertainty grows because the measured quantity is squared.

1.16 PRACTICAL GRAPH EXAMPLE
Suppose a student investigates extension x against force F for a spring. If the graph is linear through the origin, F = kx. If x is plotted vertically against F horizontally, gradient = 1/k. If F is plotted vertically against x horizontally, gradient = k. The student must state which graph was used before interpreting the gradient.

1.17 PRECISION, ACCURACY AND RESOLUTION
A ruler marked every millimetre has a finer resolution than a ruler marked every centimetre, but a fine-resolution instrument can still be systematically inaccurate if it is badly calibrated. Students should therefore never equate resolution with accuracy.

1.18 SIGNIFICANT-FIGURE EXAMPLE
If a measured distance is 2.4 m and a calculated speed is 7.846 m s⁻¹, reporting 7.846 m s⁻¹ may imply unjustified precision. A suitable rounded answer might be 7.8 m s⁻¹ if the input data justify two significant figures.

1.19 HOMOGENEITY LIMITATION
Dimensional analysis can reject an equation with incompatible units, but cannot distinguish between equations that differ only by dimensionless numerical factors. For example, v = √(gh) and v = √(2gh) have the same dimensions. Physics and derivation are needed to determine the correct coefficient.

1.20 EXAM CHECK
Whenever a numerical answer looks unreasonable, check units first, then powers of ten, then substitution, then the physical assumptions.

topic: 2.0 Newtonian Mechanics — Kinematics, Dynamics, Forces, Work, Energy, Power, Circular Motion and Gravitational Fields
content:
2.0 NEWTONIAN MECHANICS
The revised 2024–2030 syllabus includes Kinematics, Dynamics, Forces, Work Energy and Power, Circular Motion and Gravitational Field. The treatment below expands those syllabus requirements into a coherent study chapter.

2.1 KINEMATICS
Kinematics describes motion without initially considering the causes of motion.

Distance is the total path length travelled and is scalar.
Displacement is the vector change in position from initial to final position.
Speed is rate of change of distance.
Velocity is rate of change of displacement.
Acceleration is rate of change of velocity.

Average speed = total distance / total time.
Average velocity = displacement / total time.

Instantaneous velocity is the gradient of a displacement-time graph at a point.
Instantaneous acceleration is the gradient of a velocity-time graph at a point.

For constant acceleration:
v = u + at
s = ut + 1/2 at²
v² = u² + 2as
s = 1/2(u + v)t.

Here u is initial velocity, v final velocity, a acceleration, s displacement and t time.

These equations apply only when acceleration is constant.

2.2 MOTION GRAPHS
Displacement-time graph:
gradient = velocity.

Velocity-time graph:
gradient = acceleration.
area under graph = displacement.

Acceleration-time graph:
area under graph = change in velocity.

A horizontal displacement-time graph means zero velocity. A straight sloping line indicates constant velocity. A curved displacement-time graph indicates changing velocity.

Free fall near the Earth's surface is approximately uniformly accelerated if air resistance is neglected:
a = g ≈ 9.81 m s⁻² downward.

For an object released from rest:
u = 0.
Then v = gt and s = 1/2gt².

Sign conventions must be established before solving vertical-motion problems. Choose one direction as positive and retain it consistently.

2.3 PROJECTILE MOTION
A projectile has simultaneous horizontal and vertical motion after launch when air resistance is neglected.

The horizontal component has constant velocity:
ux = u cos θ.
Horizontal acceleration = 0.

The vertical component has initial velocity:
uy = u sin θ.
Vertical acceleration = −g if upward is positive.

At time t:
x = u cos θ × t
y = u sin θ × t − 1/2gt².

Horizontal and vertical motions are independent but share the same time.

At the highest point, vertical velocity is zero, but horizontal velocity remains u cos θ. Therefore acceleration is still downward with magnitude g.

For launch and landing at the same vertical level:
time of flight T = 2u sin θ/g
maximum height H = u²sin²θ/(2g)
horizontal range R = u²sin2θ/g.

The maximum range in ideal projectile motion occurs at 45° when launch and landing heights are equal and air resistance is neglected.

Real projectiles may deviate because of air resistance, wind and changing conditions.

2.4 DYNAMICS AND NEWTON'S LAWS
Dynamics explains motion in terms of forces.

Linear momentum:
p = mv.
Momentum is a vector.

Newton's first law: an object remains at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless acted upon by a resultant external force.

Newton's second law: the resultant force is equal to the rate of change of momentum. For constant mass:
F = ma.

Newton's third law: when two bodies interact, they exert forces on each other that are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. The forces act on different bodies, so they do not cancel each other on one free-body diagram.

When solving force problems:
1. identify the object;
2. draw a free-body diagram;
3. resolve forces into convenient directions;
4. calculate the resultant force;
5. apply ΣF = ma.

2.5 MOMENTUM, IMPULSE AND COLLISIONS
Conservation of momentum states that total momentum remains constant in an isolated system when resultant external impulse is zero.

For two bodies:
m1u1 + m2u2 = m1v1 + m2v2.

Elastic collision: kinetic energy is conserved as well as momentum.
Inelastic collision: momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not conserved.
Perfectly inelastic collision: bodies move together after collision.

The revised syllabus does not require coefficient-of-restitution calculations.

For a perfectly elastic one-dimensional collision:
relative speed of approach = relative speed of separation.

Impulse:
J = Δp = mv − mu.

Also:
J = FΔt for constant force,
and more generally impulse equals the area under a force-time graph.

Increasing collision time can reduce average force for a given change in momentum. This principle explains airbags, crumple zones, helmets, padding and catching techniques.

2.6 FORCES
Weight:
W = mg.
It acts vertically downward toward the centre of the Earth.

Normal reaction acts perpendicular to a contact surface.

Tension acts along a taut string or cable.

Friction opposes relative motion or the tendency of relative motion at a contact.

Drag is resistive force due to a fluid.

Upthrust is the resultant upward force exerted by a fluid on an immersed object. Pressure increases with depth, so the lower surface of an immersed object can experience greater pressure than the upper surface.

Archimedes' principle:
upthrust = weight of fluid displaced.

2.7 FRICTION AND TERMINAL VELOCITY
Friction can be useful, such as tyre-road grip and braking, but can also cause energy loss and wear.

Viscosity describes internal resistance to flow. For a small sphere moving slowly through a viscous fluid under laminar conditions, Stokes' law gives:
F = 6πηrv
where η is dynamic viscosity, r is sphere radius and v is speed.

For a falling sphere, terminal velocity occurs when the downward weight is balanced by upward forces:
weight = upthrust + viscous drag.

For a sphere:
mg = upthrust + 6πηrv_t.

Using the density form for a sphere gives:
v_t = 2r²(ρ_s − ρ_f)g/(9η).

This relation can be used to determine viscosity experimentally if the assumptions of Stokes' law are satisfied.

Typical viscosity experiment:
• use a tall transparent tube containing the liquid;
• release a small sphere;
• allow it to reach terminal speed;
• measure the time to travel a known distance;
• repeat for reliability;
• calculate v_t;
• measure sphere radius and densities;
• calculate η.

Important controls include temperature, sphere size, cleanliness and ensuring the sphere is sufficiently far from the walls.

2.8 TURNING EFFECT OF FORCES
Moment of a force about a point:
moment = force × perpendicular distance from pivot to line of action.

The SI unit is N m.

A couple consists of two equal and opposite parallel forces whose lines of action are separated. A couple produces rotation without a resultant force.

Torque of a couple:
τ = Fd
where d is perpendicular separation between the forces.

For rotational equilibrium:
sum clockwise moments = sum anticlockwise moments.

For translational equilibrium:
ΣF = 0.

A rigid body in complete equilibrium requires both zero resultant force and zero resultant moment.

Centre of gravity is the point through which the resultant weight of a body acts.

2.9 WORK, ENERGY AND POWER
Work done by a constant force:
W = Fs cos θ,
where θ is the angle between force and displacement.

If force and displacement are parallel:
W = Fs.

Work is a scalar measured in joules.

Kinetic energy:
Ek = 1/2mv².

Derivation:
From v² = u² + 2as and F = ma:
v² − u² = 2as
multiply by m/2:
1/2mv² − 1/2mu² = mas = Fs.
Thus work done equals change in kinetic energy.

Gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface:
Ep = mgh.

This follows because lifting a mass m through height h against approximately constant weight mg requires:
W = Fh = mgh.

Elastic potential energy for a Hookean spring:
E = 1/2kx².

Internal energy is the total microscopic kinetic and potential energy associated with particles within a system. It can change through heating or work done.

2.10 CONSERVATION OF ENERGY
Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it is transferred between forms.

Examples:
gravitational potential → kinetic;
chemical → thermal;
chemical → electrical;
solar radiation → electrical;
electrical → kinetic in a motor;
kinetic → electrical in a generator.

Efficiency:
efficiency = useful output energy / total input energy × 100%.
It can also be expressed using power.

Real devices lose energy, commonly as thermal energy, sound or unwanted mechanical effects. “Lost” energy is not destroyed; it has been transferred into less useful forms.

2.11 POWER
Power is rate of doing work:
P = W/t.

For a force producing motion at velocity v:
P = Fv
when force and velocity are parallel.

If not parallel:
P = Fv cos θ.

Power is measured in watts.

2.12 ENERGY TECHNOLOGIES AND ENVIRONMENT
Hydroelectric generation converts gravitational potential energy of stored water into kinetic energy, then mechanical and electrical energy.
Thermal power stations convert chemical or nuclear energy into thermal energy, mechanical energy and finally electrical energy.
Solar photovoltaic systems convert radiant energy directly into electrical energy.
Wind turbines convert kinetic energy of moving air into mechanical rotation and electrical energy.

Students should evaluate environmental and social considerations including emissions, land use, water resources, reliability, intermittency, waste, maintenance, cost and sustainability.

2.13 CIRCULAR MOTION
Angular displacement is measured in radians.
One complete revolution = 2π radians.

Angular velocity:
ω = Δθ/Δt.

Relationship between linear and angular velocity:
v = rω.

Frequency f is number of revolutions per second.
Period T is time for one revolution:
f = 1/T.

Angular speed:
ω = 2πf = 2π/T.

Uniform circular motion has constant speed but changing velocity because direction changes continuously.

Centripetal acceleration:
a = v²/r = rω².

Centripetal force:
F = mv²/r = mrω².

Centripetal force is not a new type of force; it is the resultant inward force. Depending on the situation it may be supplied by tension, friction, gravity, normal reaction or a combination.

Examples:
• friction provides centripetal force for a car turning on a flat road;
• tension can provide it for a mass on a string;
• gravity provides it for an orbiting satellite.

Banked roads allow part of the normal reaction to provide an inward component, reducing reliance on friction.

2.14 GRAVITATIONAL FIELDS
A gravitational field is a region in which a mass experiences gravitational force.

Gravitational field strength:
g = F/m.

For a point mass M:
g = GM/r².

Newton's law of gravitation:
F = Gm1m2/r².

The inverse-square relationship means that if distance from a point mass doubles, gravitational field strength becomes one quarter.

Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a small test mass from infinity to that point:
φ = −GM/r.

The potential is negative when infinity is chosen as zero because work must be done by the field to bring a positive test mass inward; equivalently, external work is negative for a slow inward transfer.

For a circular satellite orbit:
GMm/r² = mv²/r
so
v = √(GM/r).

Using v = 2πr/T:
T² = 4π²r³/(GM).

A geostationary satellite must orbit in the equatorial plane, move in the same direction as Earth's rotation, have an orbital period equal to Earth's rotation period and remain above the same point on Earth's surface.

Applications include communications, weather monitoring and remote sensing.

2.15 EXPERIMENTAL DETERMINATION OF g
A falling-body method can determine g by measuring distance and time and using:
s = 1/2gt²
for release from rest.

A graph of s against t² should be a straight line through the origin ideally, with gradient g/2.

Possible errors include reaction time, air resistance, timing resolution and uncertainty in distance.

Improvement methods include electronic timing, light gates, motion sensors, multiple distances and repeated measurements.

CORE FORMULAE
v = u + at
s = ut + 1/2at²
v² = u² + 2as
p = mv
F = ma
J = Δp
W = Fs cosθ
Ek = 1/2mv²
Ep = mgh
P = W/t
P = Fv
a_c = v²/r = rω²
F_c = mv²/r = mrω²
F = Gm1m2/r²
g = GM/r²
φ = −GM/r

2.16 WORKED EXAMPLE: UNIFORMLY ACCELERATED MOTION
A car starts from rest and accelerates at 3.0 m s⁻² for 8.0 s.
u = 0, a = 3.0 m s⁻², t = 8.0 s.
v = u + at = 24 m s⁻¹.
s = ut + 1/2at² = 96 m.
The result can be checked with v² = u² + 2as:
24² = 2(3)(96).

2.17 WORKED EXAMPLE: PROJECTILE
A projectile is launched at speed 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° above horizontal.
ux = 20 cos30°.
uy = 20 sin30° = 10 m s⁻¹.
Ignoring air resistance:
time to highest point = uy/g ≈ 1.02 s.
Maximum height = uy²/(2g) ≈ 5.10 m.
If landing at the launch level, total flight time ≈ 2.04 s.
The horizontal range is approximately 35.3 m.

2.18 FREE-BODY DIAGRAM EXAMPLE
A block is pulled horizontally across a rough surface. Forces are weight downward, normal reaction upward, applied force forward and friction backward. If vertical acceleration is zero, R = mg. If horizontal acceleration is a, applied force minus friction = ma.

2.19 COLLISION EXAMPLE
A 2 kg trolley moving at 4 m s⁻¹ collides with a 1 kg stationary trolley and they stick together.
Initial momentum = 2(4) + 1(0) = 8 kg m s⁻¹.
Total mass after collision = 3 kg.
Common speed = 8/3 ≈ 2.67 m s⁻¹.
Momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy decreases because the collision is inelastic.

2.20 IMPULSE EXAMPLE
If a 0.20 kg ball changes velocity from +15 m s⁻¹ to −10 m s⁻¹:
Δp = m(v − u) = 0.20(−10 − 15) = −5.0 N s.
The magnitude of impulse is 5.0 N s. The negative sign indicates reversal of direction.

2.21 MOMENT EXAMPLE
A 40 N force acts perpendicular to a lever at 0.30 m from the pivot.
Moment = 40 × 0.30 = 12 N m.
If a second force produces an anticlockwise moment of 12 N m, the system can be in rotational equilibrium provided the resultant force is also zero.

2.22 UPTHRUST EXAMPLE
An object displaces 0.002 m³ of water.
Taking water density as 1000 kg m⁻³:
mass displaced = ρV = 2 kg.
Weight displaced = 2g ≈ 19.6 N.
Therefore upthrust ≈ 19.6 N.

2.23 TERMINAL VELOCITY REASONING
At release, a falling sphere accelerates because weight exceeds resistive forces. As speed increases, viscous drag increases. At terminal speed, upward drag plus upthrust balances weight, so resultant force and acceleration are zero even though the sphere continues moving.

2.24 WORK-ENERGY EXAMPLE
A 2 kg object increases speed from 3 to 7 m s⁻¹.
Change in kinetic energy:
ΔEk = 1/2(2)(7² − 3²) = 40 J.
Therefore 40 J of net work is done on the object.

2.25 POWER EXAMPLE
A motor exerts a driving force of 500 N while moving at 4 m s⁻¹ in the force direction.
P = Fv = 2000 W = 2.0 kW.

2.26 CIRCULAR MOTION EXAMPLE
A 0.50 kg object moves at 6 m s⁻¹ in a circle of radius 2 m.
a_c = v²/r = 18 m s⁻².
F_c = ma = 9.0 N.
The force must point toward the centre.

2.27 GRAVITATIONAL FIELD EXAMPLE
For a point mass M, doubling r changes g = GM/r² to GM/(2r)² = one quarter of the original value. This inverse-square behaviour is central to satellite and orbital calculations.

2.28 ORBITAL SPEED
For circular orbit:
GMm/r² = mv²/r.
Cancel m:
GM/r = v².
Thus v = √(GM/r).
The satellite mass does not appear in the final expression, so all satellites at the same circular orbital radius have the same ideal orbital speed.

2.29 GRAVITATIONAL POTENTIAL
At a point r from mass M:
φ = −GM/r.
The negative sign means the point is in a bound gravitational potential relative to zero at infinity. Moving a mass from a point to infinity requires positive external work.

2.30 FORCE VS FIELD STRENGTH
Gravitational force depends on the test mass:
F = mg.
Field strength does not:
g = F/m.
Likewise, electric field strength E is force per unit positive test charge and is independent of the chosen test charge in the ideal limit.

2.31 MECHANICS PROBLEM-SOLVING ROUTINE
Draw the situation.
Choose a positive direction.
List known quantities.
Select the physical law.
Substitute consistently.
Check dimensions.
Interpret the sign.
State the final answer with unit.
source: MoPSE/ZIMSEC Physics Forms 5-6 Syllabus 2024-2030; expanded original study notes

subject: Physics
topic: 3.0 Oscillations and Waves — SHM, Progressive Waves, Stationary Waves, Diffraction and Interference
content:
3.0 OSCILLATIONS AND WAVES
The revised syllabus includes Oscillations, Waves and Superposition. The subject should be studied mathematically and physically: students must understand the motion, graphs, energy transfers, wave relationships and experimental evidence.

3.1 OSCILLATORY MOTION
Oscillation is repeated motion about an equilibrium position. Examples include a mass on a spring, a simple pendulum for small angular amplitudes and vibrating strings.

Important quantities:
Amplitude A: maximum displacement from equilibrium.
Period T: time for one complete oscillation.
Frequency f: oscillations per second.
f = 1/T.
Angular frequency:
ω = 2πf = 2π/T.

An oscillation is periodic when the motion repeats after equal intervals.

3.2 SIMPLE HARMONIC MOTION
Simple harmonic motion (SHM) is oscillatory motion in which acceleration is directly proportional to displacement from equilibrium and directed toward equilibrium:
a = −ω²x.

The negative sign indicates that acceleration is opposite to displacement.

For displacement:
x = A sin(ωt + φ)
or
x = A cos(ωt + φ),
depending on the chosen initial condition.

Velocity:
v = ±ω√(A² − x²).

Maximum speed occurs at equilibrium:
v_max = ωA.

Acceleration:
a = −ω²x.
Maximum acceleration occurs at maximum displacement:
a_max = ω²A.

3.3 MASS-SPRING SYSTEM
For a mass m attached to a spring of force constant k:
T = 2π√(m/k).

Increasing mass increases period.
Increasing stiffness k decreases period.

The equation assumes an ideal spring and small oscillations.

3.4 SIMPLE PENDULUM
For small angular oscillations:
T = 2π√(l/g).

The period is independent of the mass of the bob. It depends on length and g under the small-angle approximation.

A practical experiment can determine g:
• measure length from pivot to centre of bob;
• measure time for a large number N of oscillations;
• calculate T = t/N;
• repeat for several lengths;
• plot T² against l;
• from T² = (4π²/g)l, gradient = 4π²/g;
• hence g = 4π²/gradient.

Sources of uncertainty include reaction time, uncertainty in effective length, large amplitude and counting errors.

3.5 ENERGY IN SHM
In ideal SHM, total mechanical energy remains constant.

At maximum displacement:
velocity = 0,
kinetic energy = 0,
potential energy is maximum.

At equilibrium:
displacement = 0,
speed is maximum,
kinetic energy is maximum.

For a spring:
E_total = 1/2kA² = 1/2mω²A².

Real oscillators experience damping. Mechanical energy is transferred to thermal energy and other forms, so amplitude decreases.

3.6 DAMPING
Damping is the reduction of amplitude due to resistive forces.

Light damping: oscillations continue for many cycles with gradually decreasing amplitude.
Critical damping: system returns to equilibrium rapidly without oscillating.
Heavy/overdamping: return to equilibrium is slower without oscillation.

Applications include vehicle suspension, door closers and instrument damping.

3.7 FORCED OSCILLATIONS AND RESONANCE
A forced oscillator is driven by an external periodic force.

Resonance occurs when the driving frequency is close to the natural frequency, producing a large amplitude response.

Damping reduces the maximum resonant amplitude and broadens the response curve.

Resonance is useful in musical instruments, tuning circuits and sensors, but potentially dangerous in bridges, buildings and rotating machinery.

3.8 PROGRESSIVE WAVES
A progressive wave transfers energy and information from one location to another without an overall transfer of matter with the wave.

Amplitude is maximum displacement.
Wavelength λ is distance between adjacent points in phase.
Frequency f is oscillations per second.
Period T = 1/f.
Wave speed:
v = fλ.

Phase difference between points separated by distance Δx:
phase difference = 2πΔx/λ radians.

Transverse waves have oscillations perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer. Examples include electromagnetic waves.
Longitudinal waves have oscillations parallel to energy transfer. Sound in air is longitudinal.

3.9 WAVE PROPERTIES
Reflection occurs when a wave encounters a boundary and returns.
Refraction is change in direction due to a change in wave speed when entering a different medium.
Diffraction is spreading around obstacles or through apertures.
Interference results from superposition of waves.

Frequency is determined by the source and does not change simply because a wave enters a new medium. Speed and wavelength may change.

3.10 SOUND AND STATIONARY WAVES
Sound waves are longitudinal mechanical waves and require a medium.

Stationary waves can form when incident and reflected waves of the same frequency and appropriate phase relationship superpose.

Nodes are points of zero displacement.
Antinodes are points of maximum displacement.

Adjacent nodes are separated by λ/2.
Adjacent antinodes are separated by λ/2.
A node and nearest antinode are separated by λ/4.

For a string fixed at both ends:
L = nλ/2,
where n = 1,2,3,...

For an open pipe, ideal modes are similarly related to half-wavelength sections. For a closed pipe, only odd harmonics occur under the ideal model.

3.11 MEASURING THE WAVELENGTH OF SOUND USING STATIONARY WAVES
A resonance tube can be used to determine wavelength. Vary the effective length until strong resonance occurs. The separation between successive resonance positions can be used to determine λ/2, depending on the apparatus and end correction.

A signal generator and speaker can provide a controlled frequency. A microphone or suitable detector can identify resonance.

Always account for end correction where the apparatus requires it.

3.12 SUPERPOSITION
When two or more waves overlap, the resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of individual displacements.

Constructive interference occurs when waves arrive in phase.
Destructive interference occurs when they arrive out of phase.

For two coherent sources, coherence requires a constant phase relationship and the same frequency.

3.13 YOUNG'S TWO-SOURCE INTERFERENCE
Young's experiment demonstrates interference using coherent light sources.

Bright fringes occur when path difference:
δ = nλ.

Dark fringes occur when:
δ = (n + 1/2)λ.

Fringe spacing:
x = λD/a
where x is fringe separation, D is distance from sources to screen and a is source separation.

Assumptions include small angles and a suitable coherent source arrangement.

Increasing λ increases fringe spacing.
Increasing D increases fringe spacing.
Increasing a decreases fringe spacing.

3.14 DIFFRACTION
Diffraction is spreading of waves as they pass through an aperture or around an obstacle. It is strongest when aperture size is comparable with wavelength.

For a diffraction grating:
d sinθ = nλ
where d is grating spacing, θ is diffraction angle and n is order.

If a grating has N lines per metre:
d = 1/N.

Higher wavelength generally gives larger diffraction angles for the same order and grating spacing.

3.15 POLARISATION
Polarisation applies to transverse waves. It can therefore demonstrate the transverse nature of electromagnetic waves.

A polariser restricts oscillation direction. Two polarising filters transmit maximum intensity when their transmission axes are parallel and minimum when perpendicular.

Malus-type relationships may be used when included in a specified experimental context, but students should not assume an equation unless it is part of the required syllabus/formula data.

3.16 GRAPH AND PRACTICAL SKILLS
For wave experiments:
• identify independent/dependent variables;
• control temperature and apparatus geometry;
• measure several wavelengths or frequencies;
• repeat readings;
• calculate means;
• plot linearised graphs;
• determine gradient;
• estimate uncertainty;
• discuss systematic effects such as end correction.

3.17 COMMON EXAM TRAPS
Do not confuse amplitude with wavelength.
Do not state that a wave “carries matter” as a general rule.
Do not say frequency changes merely because speed changes at a boundary.
Do not call a node a point of zero energy; it is a point of zero displacement in the stationary-wave pattern, while energy transfer through an ideal stationary wave is not the same as progressive-wave energy transport.
Do not confuse diffraction with refraction.
For interference, coherence is essential for a stable fringe pattern.

CORE FORMULAE
f = 1/T
ω = 2πf
v = fλ
a = −ω²x
v_max = ωA
a_max = ω²A
T_spring = 2π√(m/k)
T_pendulum = 2π√(l/g)
x = λD/a
d sinθ = nλ

3.18 SHM WORKED EXAMPLE
A mass performs SHM with amplitude 0.040 m and angular frequency 5.0 rad s⁻¹.
Maximum speed:
v_max = ωA = 5(0.040) = 0.20 m s⁻¹.
Maximum acceleration:
a_max = ω²A = 25(0.040) = 1.0 m s⁻².

3.19 SHM AT A GENERAL POSITION
At x = A/2:
v = ω√(A² − A²/4)
= ωA√3/2.
Thus the speed is about 0.866 of maximum speed.

3.20 SPRING PERIOD
If m = 0.50 kg and k = 200 N m⁻¹:
T = 2π√(0.50/200) ≈ 0.314 s.
Increasing the mass to 2.0 kg would double the period because T ∝ √m.

3.21 PENDULUM GRAPH
From:
T = 2π√(l/g)
square both sides:
T² = (4π²/g)l.
Therefore a T² against l graph is linear. The gradient equals 4π²/g, so g = 4π²/gradient.

3.22 ENERGY IN SHM
For a spring of k = 100 N m⁻¹ and amplitude 0.10 m:
E = 1/2kA² = 0.50 J.
At equilibrium the kinetic energy is 0.50 J and the elastic potential energy is zero in the ideal model.

3.23 WAVE EQUATION
If a wave has frequency 500 Hz and wavelength 0.68 m:
v = fλ = 340 m s⁻¹.
This is consistent with a typical speed of sound in air under suitable conditions.

3.24 PHASE DIFFERENCE
Two points separated by λ/4 have phase difference π/2 radians, or 90°.
Two points separated by λ/2 have phase difference π radians, or 180°.
Points separated by λ are in phase.

3.25 STATIONARY WAVE
If the distance between adjacent nodes is 0.25 m, then:
λ/2 = 0.25 m,
so λ = 0.50 m.
If frequency is 680 Hz, wave speed = 340 m s⁻¹.

3.26 YOUNG INTERFERENCE EXAMPLE
Suppose λ = 600 nm, D = 2.0 m and slit separation a = 0.50 mm.
x = λD/a
= (600 × 10⁻9 × 2)/(0.50 × 10⁻3)
= 2.4 × 10⁻3 m
= 2.4 mm.
Always convert nanometres and millimetres to SI units.

3.27 DIFFRACTION GRATING EXAMPLE
A grating has 600 lines per mm. Convert:
600 lines/mm = 600,000 lines/m.
d = 1/N = 1.67 × 10⁻6 m.
Then use d sinθ = nλ for the required order.

3.28 RESONANCE
At resonance, the driving frequency is close to the natural frequency and the oscillator receives energy efficiently from the driving force. Damping reduces the maximum amplitude. A practical answer should explain energy transfer, not simply state “amplitude increases”.

3.29 REFLECTION, REFRACTION AND DIFFRACTION
Reflection changes direction at a boundary while remaining in the original medium.
Refraction occurs when wave speed changes on entering a different medium.
Diffraction is spreading associated with finite apertures or obstacles.
Interference is a result of superposition and can occur wherever coherent waves overlap.

3.30 PRACTICAL WAVE CHECKLIST
Measure several cycles rather than one where possible.
Keep frequency stable when measuring wavelength.
Record resonance positions carefully.
Control geometry.
Use graphs where they reveal a relationship.
State whether end correction is relevant.
source: MoPSE/ZIMSEC Physics Forms 5-6 Syllabus 2024-2030; expanded original study notes

subject: Physics
topic: 4.0 Electricity and Magnetism — Charge, D.C. Circuits, Electric Fields, Capacitance, Electromagnetism, Induction and A.C.
content:
4.0 ELECTRICITY AND MAGNETISM
The revised syllabus places Electricity, D.C. Circuits, Electric Fields and Capacitance in Form 5, followed by Electromagnetism, Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents in Form 6.

4.1 ELECTRIC CHARGE AND CURRENT
Electric charge is measured in coulombs (C). Elementary charge:
e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

Current is rate of flow of charge:
I = Q/t
for constant current, or I = dQ/dt instantaneously.

Conventional current is defined as flow of positive charge and is opposite to electron drift in metallic conductors.

Potential difference is work done per unit charge:
V = W/Q.

Electromotive force (emf) is energy supplied by a source per unit charge passing through the source.

Resistance:
R = V/I.

Ohm's law states that for an ohmic conductor under constant physical conditions, current is proportional to potential difference.

4.2 RESISTIVITY
For a uniform conductor:
R = ρL/A.
ρ is resistivity in Ω m.

Resistance increases with length and decreases with cross-sectional area, assuming resistivity remains constant.

Temperature affects resistance. For metallic conductors, resistance generally increases as temperature rises.

4.3 SERIES AND PARALLEL CIRCUITS
Series:
same current through each component.
Total resistance:
R_total = R1 + R2 + ...

Parallel:
same potential difference across each branch.
1/R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ...

For a source of emf E and internal resistance r supplying current I:
E = V + Ir,
where V is terminal potential difference.

Terminal p.d.:
V = E − Ir.

Internal resistance can be determined experimentally from a graph of terminal voltage V against current I:
V = E − Ir.
Gradient = −r.
Intercept = E.

4.4 KIRCHHOFF'S LAWS
Kirchhoff's first law: total current entering a junction equals total current leaving the junction. It follows from conservation of charge.

Kirchhoff's second law: the algebraic sum of potential changes around a closed loop is zero. It follows from conservation of energy.

When applying loop equations, choose a sign convention and use it consistently.

4.5 ELECTRICAL POWER AND ENERGY
Power:
P = IV.
Also:
P = I²R
and
P = V²/R.

Electrical energy:
E = Pt = IVt.

For household energy use, energy may be measured in kilowatt-hours:
1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

4.6 POTENTIOMETER AND MEASUREMENT
A potentiometer can compare potential differences accurately because at balance no current is drawn from the test source in the ideal arrangement.

It can be used to compare emf, determine internal resistance and calibrate meters.

4.7 ELECTRIC FIELDS
An electric field is a region where a charge experiences an electric force.

Electric field strength:
E = F/Q.

For a point charge Q:
E = Q/(4πε₀r²).

Electric force between point charges:
F = Q1Q2/(4πε₀r²).

Electric potential:
V = W/Q.

Potential due to a point charge:
V = Q/(4πε₀r).

Field direction is defined as the direction of force on a positive test charge.

For a uniform field:
E = V/d
where d is separation of equipotential surfaces/plates when field is uniform.

4.8 ELECTRIC POTENTIAL ENERGY
The potential energy of a charge q at electric potential V is:
U = qV.

For two point charges:
U = Qq/(4πε₀r).

Positive and negative charges require careful sign handling.

4.9 ELECTRIC FIELD LINES
Field lines:
• point in the direction of force on a positive test charge;
• never cross;
• are closer together where field is stronger;
• for isolated point charges radiate radially;
• terminate on negative charge or extend to infinity depending on the system.

4.10 CAPACITANCE
Capacitance measures charge stored per unit potential difference:
C = Q/V.

Unit: farad (F).

A capacitor stores energy in an electric field.

For capacitors in parallel:
C_total = C1 + C2 + ...

For capacitors in series:
1/C_total = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + ...

Energy stored:
W = 1/2QV
= 1/2CV²
= Q²/(2C).

For a parallel-plate capacitor:
C = εA/d
for a suitable dielectric arrangement.

Increasing plate area increases capacitance.
Increasing separation decreases capacitance.
A dielectric increases capacitance by reducing effective electric field for a given charge and allowing more charge to be stored at the same voltage.

4.11 CHARGING AND DISCHARGING RC CIRCUITS
In a series resistor-capacitor circuit, the capacitor charges gradually rather than instantaneously.

Time constant:
τ = RC.

During charging from a constant source E:
V_C = E(1 − e^(−t/RC)).
Q = CE(1 − e^(−t/RC)).
I = (E/R)e^(−t/RC).

During discharge from initial voltage V₀:
V_C = V₀e^(−t/RC).
Q = Q₀e^(−t/RC).
I magnitude decreases exponentially.

At t = RC during charging, capacitor voltage has reached approximately 63% of final value. During discharge, approximately 37% remains.

4.12 MAGNETIC FIELDS
A magnetic field is a region in which a moving charge, current-carrying conductor or magnetic material can experience a magnetic effect.

Magnetic flux density B is force per unit current per unit length for a conductor perpendicular to the field:
B = F/(IL).

Unit: tesla (T).

For a current-carrying conductor:
F = BIL sinθ.

Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction of force for a current in a magnetic field.

For a moving charged particle:
F = Bqv sinθ.

The force is perpendicular to the velocity and field, so it can change direction without doing work on the particle in an ideal magnetic field.

4.13 ELECTROMAGNETIC INDUCTION
Electromagnetic induction is production of an emf when magnetic flux linkage changes.

Faraday's law:
induced emf ∝ rate of change of magnetic flux linkage.

Lenz's law states that the induced effect opposes the change producing it.

Magnetic flux:
Φ = BA cosθ.

Flux linkage = NΦ for N turns.

For a coil:
E = −N dΦ/dt.

The negative sign expresses Lenz's law.

Applications include generators, transformers, induction cookers and some sensors.

4.14 AC GENERATION
A rotating coil in a magnetic field can generate an alternating emf.

For sinusoidal voltage:
v = V₀ sinωt.

RMS voltage:
V_rms = V₀/√2
for a sinusoidal waveform.

Similarly:
I_rms = I₀/√2.

The RMS value is the value of steady DC that would produce the same heating effect in a resistor.

4.15 TRANSFORMERS
For an ideal transformer:
V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p.

Also:
V_pI_p = V_sI_s.

A step-up transformer has N_s > N_p.
A step-down transformer has N_s < N_p.

Transformers require changing current/flux and therefore operate with AC rather than steady DC in the ordinary transformer principle.

Power transmission uses high voltage to reduce current for a given transmitted power:
P = VI.
For a fixed power, increasing V decreases I. Since cable loss is approximately I²R, reducing current greatly reduces transmission losses.

4.16 ELECTROMAGNETIC APPLICATIONS
Electric motors convert electrical energy to mechanical energy using force on current-carrying conductors.
Generators convert mechanical energy into electrical energy through electromagnetic induction.
Relays use electromagnets to control circuits.
Loudspeakers and microphones use electromagnetic principles.

4.17 A.C. CIRCUIT IDEAS
In resistive AC circuits, current and voltage are in phase.
For capacitive and inductive circuits, phase relationships differ and energy may be temporarily stored in electric or magnetic fields.

Students should distinguish peak, peak-to-peak and RMS quantities.

4.18 PRACTICALS
Potential difference/current experiment:
• assemble circuit;
• vary supply or resistance;
• measure V and I;
• calculate R;
• plot V against I;
• determine gradient.

Internal resistance:
• vary load;
• measure terminal V and I;
• plot V against I;
• use V = E − Ir.

Capacitance:
• charge capacitor through known resistor;
• record V or I at regular intervals;
• test exponential behaviour;
• determine time constant.

Electromagnetic induction:
• move magnet through coil or coil through magnetic field;
• observe induced emf;
• reverse motion and note reversal;
• increase speed or number of turns and observe increased emf.

4.19 SAFETY
Electrical work requires suitable current limiting, insulated connections, low-voltage supplies where possible, dry hands, avoidance of short circuits and safe capacitor discharge before handling.

CORE FORMULAE
I = Q/t
V = W/Q
R = V/I
R = ρL/A
P = IV = I²R = V²/R
E = Pt
E_field = F/Q
E_point = Q/(4πε₀r²)
V_point = Q/(4πε₀r)
C = Q/V
W_C = 1/2QV = 1/2CV²
τ = RC
F = BIL sinθ
F = Bqv sinθ
Φ = BA cosθ
E_induced = −N dΦ/dt
V_rms = V₀/√2
V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p

4.20 CIRCUIT EXAMPLE
A 12 V supply is connected to a 6 Ω resistor.
I = V/R = 2.0 A.
Power = VI = 24 W.
Energy used in 5 minutes:
E = Pt = 24 × 300 = 7200 J.

4.21 SERIES/PARALLEL EXAMPLE
Two 6 Ω resistors in series:
R = 12 Ω.
Connected in parallel:
1/R = 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3,
so R = 3 Ω.

4.22 INTERNAL RESISTANCE EXAMPLE
A cell has emf 1.50 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω. If current is 1.0 A:
V_terminal = E − Ir = 1.50 − 0.50 = 1.00 V.

4.23 ELECTRIC FIELD EXAMPLE
For a point charge, field strength varies as 1/r². If distance changes from r to 3r, the field becomes 1/9 of its original value.

4.24 ELECTRIC POTENTIAL EXAMPLE
At a point r from a positive point charge Q:
V = Q/(4πε₀r).
Potential is scalar, so contributions from several point charges can be added algebraically with signs.

4.25 CAPACITOR EXAMPLE
A 100 μF capacitor is charged to 12 V.
Q = CV = 100 × 10⁻6 × 12 = 1.2 × 10⁻3 C.
Energy:
W = 1/2CV²
= 0.5(100 × 10⁻6)(144)
= 7.2 × 10⁻3 J.

4.26 RC TIME CONSTANT
If R = 100 kΩ and C = 10 μF:
τ = RC = (100 × 10³)(10 × 10⁻6) = 1.0 s.
After one time constant during charging, the capacitor voltage is approximately 63% of final value.

4.27 MAGNETIC FORCE EXAMPLE
A 0.40 m conductor carries 5 A perpendicular to a magnetic field of 0.20 T.
F = BIL = 0.20 × 5 × 0.40 = 0.40 N.

4.28 CHARGED PARTICLE
A particle moving perpendicular to B experiences:
F = qvB.
Equating this to mv²/r:
r = mv/(qB).
Increasing momentum increases radius. Increasing charge magnitude or magnetic field strength decreases radius.

4.29 ELECTROMAGNETIC INDUCTION
A larger induced emf can result from:
• increasing the number of turns;
• increasing rate of change of magnetic flux;
• increasing magnetic field strength;
• increasing coil area where appropriate;
• moving the magnet/coil faster.

The direction follows Lenz's law.

4.30 TRANSFORMER EXAMPLE
If Np = 1000 turns, Ns = 200 turns and Vp = 240 V:
Vs/Vp = Ns/Np = 0.2.
Vs = 48 V.
For an ideal transformer, input and output power are equal, so current increases on the low-voltage side.

4.31 POWER TRANSMISSION
For 1 MW transmitted:
at 10 kV, I = 100 A.
At 100 kV, I = 10 A.
For the same line resistance, I²R losses are reduced by a factor of 100 when current is reduced by a factor of 10.

4.32 RMS
For a sinusoidal source with peak voltage 325 V:
V_rms = 325/√2 ≈ 230 V.
This explains why a nominal 230 V AC supply has a higher instantaneous peak voltage.

4.33 KIRCHHOFF METHOD
Choose current directions arbitrarily.
Apply junction law.
Choose loop direction.
Write potential rises and drops consistently.
Solve simultaneous equations.
A negative current result means the actual current direction is opposite to the assumed direction.

4.34 CAPACITOR PRACTICAL
A graph of ln(V) against t during discharge can be linear because:
V = V₀e^(−t/RC)
ln V = ln V₀ − t/RC.
Gradient = −1/RC.
This allows the time constant to be determined experimentally.

4.35 ELECTRICAL SAFETY
Even low-voltage circuits can produce high currents during a short circuit. Capacitors can retain charge after a supply is disconnected. Always discharge capacitors safely and observe the voltage/current ratings of components.

subject: Physics
topic: 5.0 Electronics — Analogue Electronics, Operational Amplifiers, Digital Electronics and Communication Foundations
content:
5.0 ELECTRONICS
The revised 2024–2030 syllabus includes Analogue Electronics and Digital Electronics. Electronics should be studied as the controlled processing of electrical signals using components and systems.

5.1 ANALOGUE SIGNALS
An analogue signal varies continuously with time and can have continuously varying amplitude. Examples include microphone output and many sensor signals.

Important signal properties:
amplitude;
frequency;
period;
phase;
bandwidth.

Sensors/transducers convert a physical quantity into an electrical signal or vice versa.

Examples:
thermistor: temperature-sensitive resistance;
LDR: light-sensitive resistance;
microphone: sound to electrical signal;
photodiode: light to electrical current;
strain gauge: deformation to resistance change.

5.2 DIODES
A diode conducts preferentially in one direction.

A semiconductor diode has a forward-biased low-resistance state and a reverse-biased high-resistance state, subject to breakdown and device limits.

Applications:
• rectification;
• protection;
• switching;
• signal detection.

LEDs emit light when forward biased and are used as indicators and displays. They require current limiting in ordinary circuits.

A photodiode responds to incident light and is commonly operated with reverse bias in sensing applications.

5.3 TRANSISTORS
A transistor can operate as an amplifier or electronic switch.

In a simple transistor switch:
cut-off corresponds approximately to OFF;
saturation corresponds approximately to ON.

Amplification means a small input signal controls a larger output signal using energy supplied by the power source.

Students should distinguish voltage gain, current gain and power gain.

5.4 OPERATIONAL AMPLIFIERS
An ideal operational amplifier has:
• very high open-loop voltage gain;
• very high input resistance;
• very low output resistance;
• very wide bandwidth in the ideal approximation;
• negligible input current;
• zero differential input voltage when negative feedback keeps the amplifier in its linear region.

The ideal op-amp is often treated as having:
V+ ≈ V− under negative feedback,
I+ ≈ I− ≈ 0.

5.5 INVERTING AMPLIFIER
For an ideal inverting amplifier:
V_out = −(R_f/R_in)V_in.

Voltage gain:
A_v = −R_f/R_in.

The negative sign indicates phase inversion.

Using the virtual-earth approximation, the inverting input is approximately at 0 V when the non-inverting input is grounded and negative feedback is operating.

5.6 NON-INVERTING AMPLIFIER
For an ideal non-inverting amplifier:
A_v = 1 + R_f/R_1.

Output is in phase with input.

5.7 VOLTAGE FOLLOWER
A voltage follower is a non-inverting unity-gain buffer:
V_out ≈ V_in.

It provides high input impedance and low output impedance, allowing one circuit stage to drive another without significant loading.

5.8 COMPARATOR
An operational amplifier without linear negative feedback can be used as a comparator.

If V+ > V−, output tends toward the positive saturation level.
If V+ < V−, output tends toward the negative/low saturation level.

Comparators are useful in threshold detection, alarms and control systems.

5.9 SUMMING AMPLIFIER
An inverting summing amplifier can add several input voltages with weighted contributions:
V_out = −R_f(V_1/R_1 + V_2/R_2 + ...).

It is used in analogue signal processing.

5.10 FEEDBACK
Negative feedback reduces gain but improves stability, linearity and bandwidth in appropriate amplifier systems.

Positive feedback reinforces changes and can produce switching, oscillation or hysteresis.

5.11 SCHMITT TRIGGER
A Schmitt trigger uses positive feedback to create hysteresis. It has different switching thresholds for rising and falling input signals.

This prevents noisy input signals from causing rapid unwanted switching.

5.12 DIGITAL ELECTRONICS
Digital systems represent information using discrete levels, commonly binary 0 and 1.

Logic gates:
NOT: output is opposite input.
AND: output is 1 only if all inputs are 1.
OR: output is 1 if at least one input is 1.
NAND: NOT-AND.
NOR: NOT-OR.
XOR: output is 1 when inputs differ.

Truth tables should be constructed carefully.

5.13 BOOLEAN IDEAS
Basic operations:
AND = multiplication-like operation.
OR = addition-like operation subject to Boolean rules.
NOT = inversion.

Useful identities:
A AND 1 = A
A AND 0 = 0
A OR 0 = A
A OR 1 = 1
NOT(NOT A) = A.

De Morgan's laws:
NOT(A AND B) = NOT A OR NOT B.
NOT(A OR B) = NOT A AND NOT B.

5.14 LOGIC CIRCUITS
A logic circuit can be simplified by Boolean algebra or truth-table analysis.

When designing:
1. identify inputs and outputs;
2. state desired behaviour;
3. construct truth table;
4. derive Boolean expression;
5. simplify;
6. draw gate circuit;
7. test.

5.15 FLIP-FLOPS AND MEMORY CONCEPTS
A flip-flop is a bistable digital circuit capable of storing one bit. It has two stable states and can change state in response to control signals.

The concept is important for counters, registers and digital memory.

5.16 ADC AND DAC
An analogue-to-digital converter samples an analogue signal and represents its values digitally.

Sampling frequency determines how frequently the analogue signal is measured. To reproduce a signal faithfully, sampling frequency must be sufficiently high relative to the highest frequency present.

Bit depth determines the number of quantisation levels:
number of levels = 2^n
for n bits.

More bits reduce quantisation step size and improve amplitude resolution.

A digital-to-analogue converter reconstructs an analogue output from digital data.

5.17 SAMPLING AND QUANTISATION
Sampling converts continuous time into discrete measurement times.
Quantisation converts continuous amplitude into discrete levels.
Encoding represents the levels in binary.

Undersampling can produce aliasing, where high-frequency information is incorrectly represented as lower-frequency behaviour.

5.18 DIGITAL ADVANTAGES
Digital systems can offer:
• good noise immunity;
• reproducible processing;
• easy storage;
• error detection/correction;
• programmable operation.

Disadvantages include quantisation error, sampling requirements, conversion circuitry and processing/storage requirements.

5.19 COMMUNICATION SYSTEM BLOCK DIAGRAM
A basic communication chain:
information source → transducer → transmitter → channel → receiver → output transducer.

Modulation can place information onto a carrier suitable for transmission.

Noise is unwanted disturbance added to a signal.

Amplification increases signal amplitude, while regeneration can reconstruct a digital signal.

5.20 OUTPUT DEVICES
The revised syllabus includes output devices such as LEDs, buzzers and relays in control-system contexts.

LED: visual indication.
Buzzer: audible indication.
Relay: electrically controlled switch allowing one circuit to control another.

5.21 OPERATIONAL AMPLIFIER PRACTICAL
For an inverting amplifier:
• build the circuit using appropriate resistor values;
• supply the op-amp safely;
• apply a small input;
• measure output;
• calculate gain;
• compare measured gain with −R_f/R_in;
• investigate saturation if input is increased.

Safety and polarity of the power supply are critical.

5.22 EXAM FOCUS
Be able to distinguish:
• analogue vs digital;
• amplifier vs comparator;
• positive vs negative feedback;
• sensor vs actuator;
• ADC vs DAC;
• voltage gain vs power gain;
• ideal op-amp assumptions vs real-device limitations.

CORE FORMULAE
A_v(inverting) = −R_f/R_in
A_v(non-inverting) = 1 + R_f/R_1
N_levels = 2^n

5.23 INVERTING AMPLIFIER EXAMPLE
R_in = 10 kΩ and R_f = 100 kΩ.
Gain = −100/10 = −10.
For input 0.20 V, ideal output = −2.0 V, provided the op-amp supply rails allow this output.

5.24 NON-INVERTING EXAMPLE
R_1 = 10 kΩ and R_f = 90 kΩ.
Gain = 1 + 90/10 = 10.
An input of 0.30 V gives an ideal output of 3.0 V if the op-amp remains within its output range.

5.25 COMPARATOR
If the reference input is 2.0 V and the signal input is 2.5 V, determine output according to which terminal receives the signal and which receives the reference. Always inspect the circuit rather than memorising one universal “high/low” statement.

5.26 ADC EXAMPLE
For an 8-bit converter:
number of levels = 2⁸ = 256.
For a 10-bit converter:
2¹⁰ = 1024 levels.
The 10-bit converter can distinguish finer amplitude changes over the same input range.

5.27 SAMPLING
If a signal contains frequencies up to 10 kHz, a sampling rate must be sufficiently above 20 kHz for ideal Nyquist-style sampling. In practical systems a margin and anti-aliasing filter are used.

5.28 LOGIC EXAMPLE
For an AND gate, inputs A=1 and B=0 produce output 0.
For an OR gate, A=1 and B=0 produce 1.
For XOR, A=1 and B=0 produce 1.
For NAND, A=1 and B=1 produce 0.

5.29 TRUTH-TABLE METHOD
List every possible input combination.
Evaluate the circuit one gate at a time.
Record intermediate outputs if necessary.
Record the final output.
Compare the result with the required specification.

5.30 FEEDBACK EXAMPLE
Negative feedback can reduce closed-loop gain but make the gain more stable against component variations. It can also increase usable bandwidth and reduce distortion in appropriate amplifier designs.

5.31 SENSOR INTERFACE
A thermistor can form part of a potential divider. Temperature changes resistance, changing output voltage. A comparator can compare this voltage with a reference and switch an alarm when a threshold is crossed.

5.32 DIGITAL VS ANALOGUE
Analogue:
continuous representation;
simple sensor interfaces;
susceptible to accumulated noise.
Digital:
discrete representation;
easy storage/processing;
can be regenerated;
requires sampling/quantisation for analogue sources.

5.33 PRACTICAL OP-AMP CHECKS
Use common reference/ground correctly.
Confirm supply polarity.
Keep input voltages within safe limits.
Avoid shorting outputs.
Do not assume the ideal equations apply when the amplifier is saturated.
Measure both input and output rather than relying only on nominal resistor values.
source: MoPSE/ZIMSEC Physics Forms 5-6 Syllabus 2024-2030; expanded original study notes

topic: 7.0 Matter — Phases, Deformation, Temperature, Thermal Properties, Ideal Gases, Fluids and Thermal Energy Transfer
content:
7.0 MATTER
The revised syllabus covers Phases of Matter, Deformation of Solids, Temperature, Thermal Properties of Materials, Ideal Gases, Non-viscous Fluid Flow and Transfer of Thermal Energy.

7.1 PARTICLE MODEL OF MATTER
Matter consists of particles in continuous motion. The behaviour of a substance depends on particle arrangement, separation and interaction.

Solid:
particles closely packed in an ordered or structured arrangement; strong interactions; fixed shape and volume; particles vibrate around equilibrium positions.

Liquid:
particles remain close but can move relative to one another; fixed volume but no fixed shape.

Gas:
particles widely separated; weak average interactions; no fixed shape or volume; readily compressible.

7.2 CHANGES OF STATE
Melting: solid to liquid.
Freezing: liquid to solid.
Vaporisation: liquid to gas.
Condensation: gas to liquid.
Sublimation: solid to gas.
Deposition: gas to solid.

During a change of state, supplied energy can change intermolecular potential energy rather than increasing temperature. This explains why temperature can remain approximately constant during melting or boiling under constant pressure.

7.3 INTERNAL ENERGY
Internal energy is the sum of microscopic kinetic and potential energies of particles.

Heating can increase internal energy.
Work done on a system can also increase internal energy.

Temperature is related to average random kinetic energy, while internal energy includes both kinetic and interaction/potential contributions.

7.4 SPECIFIC HEAT CAPACITY
Specific heat capacity c is the energy required to raise the temperature of unit mass of a substance by one kelvin without phase change.

Q = mcΔT.

High specific heat capacity means more energy is required for a given temperature rise.

7.5 SPECIFIC LATENT HEAT
Specific latent heat is energy required per unit mass to change state without changing temperature.

Q = mL.

Specific latent heat of fusion concerns solid-liquid change.
Specific latent heat of vaporisation concerns liquid-gas change.

7.6 DEFORMATION OF SOLIDS
When a force is applied to a solid, it may deform.

Elastic deformation is reversible when the load is removed within the elastic limit.
Plastic deformation is permanent.

Tensile stress:
stress = F/A.

Strain:
strain = ΔL/L.

Strain has no unit.

Young modulus:
E = stress/strain.

For a material obeying Hooke's law:
F = kx
within the elastic region.

7.7 FORCE-EXTENSION GRAPHS
For a spring:
the gradient of force-extension graph is spring constant k.

Elastic potential energy is the area under the force-extension graph:
E = 1/2Fx for a linear spring
= 1/2kx².

For a material, the area under a stress-strain graph represents energy per unit volume associated with deformation.

7.8 BRITTLE AND DUCTILE MATERIALS
A ductile material undergoes substantial plastic deformation before fracture.
A brittle material fractures with little plastic deformation.

Design choices depend on required strength, stiffness, toughness, mass, temperature and environment.

7.9 TEMPERATURE
Temperature is a measure associated with thermal state and equilibrium. Thermometers require a thermometric property that changes predictably with temperature.

Kelvin scale:
T(K) = θ(°C) + 273.15.

Absolute zero is 0 K.

7.10 THERMAL EXPANSION
Heating generally increases average particle separation and causes expansion.

For linear expansion:
ΔL = αLΔT
where α is coefficient of linear expansion.

Applications:
bimetallic strips;
expansion joints;
thermostats;
railway tracks;
bridges.

7.11 IDEAL GAS
An ideal gas model assumes:
• particles occupy negligible volume compared with container;
• no intermolecular forces except during collisions;
• collisions are elastic;
• particles move randomly;
• collision time is negligible.

Equation:
pV = nRT.

Also:
pV = NkT
where N is number of molecules.

R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.

7.12 GAS LAWS
At constant temperature:
pV = constant.

At constant pressure:
V/T = constant.

At constant volume:
p/T = constant.

Combined:
pV/T = constant for a fixed amount of gas.

Temperatures in gas-law calculations must be in kelvin.

7.13 KINETIC THEORY
Gas pressure results from collisions of particles with container walls.

Higher temperature means greater average molecular kinetic energy.

For an ideal gas:
average translational kinetic energy per molecule = 3/2 kT.

The root-mean-square speed relationship can be expressed as:
v_rms = √(3kT/m)
for molecular mass m.

At the same temperature, lighter molecules have higher typical speeds.

7.14 HYDROSTATIC PRESSURE
Pressure:
p = F/A.

Pressure due to a liquid column:
p = ρgh
for gauge pressure relative to the surface.

Total pressure may include atmospheric pressure:
p_total = p_atm + ρgh.

7.15 NON-VISCOUS FLUID FLOW
For steady incompressible flow:
A v = constant.

This is the continuity equation.

If cross-sectional area decreases, fluid speed increases.

Bernoulli's principle for ideal steady flow:
p + 1/2ρv² + ρgh = constant
along a streamline.

This explains relationships between pressure, speed and height in ideal fluid flow.

7.16 APPLICATIONS OF FLUID FLOW
Examples include:
Venturi meters;
atomisers;
aircraft lift models;
flow measurement;
water systems.

Real fluids have viscosity and energy losses, so ideal Bernoulli predictions may require correction.

7.17 THERMAL CONDUCTION
Conduction transfers thermal energy through interactions between neighbouring particles without bulk motion of the material.

Metals are generally good thermal conductors because mobile electrons contribute to energy transfer.

Insulators reduce thermal transfer by limiting conduction and often trapping air.

7.18 CONVECTION
Convection transfers thermal energy by bulk movement of a fluid.

Heating causes density changes and buoyancy-driven circulation in many situations.

Examples:
boiling water;
room heating;
atmospheric circulation.

7.19 THERMAL RADIATION
Thermal radiation is electromagnetic radiation emitted by matter due to its temperature.

It does not require a material medium.

Dark, matt surfaces are generally good absorbers and emitters.
Shiny surfaces are generally poorer absorbers and emitters and good reflectors.

7.20 THERMAL INSULATION
Methods include:
foam;
fibreglass;
air gaps;
reflective surfaces;
double glazing.

A good insulation design considers conduction, convection, radiation and moisture.

7.21 THERMAL EXPERIMENTS
Specific heat capacity:
• measure mass;
• supply known electrical energy;
• measure temperature rise;
• calculate c = E/(mΔT);
• account for energy losses.

Latent heat:
• supply known energy during a phase change;
• measure mass changed;
• calculate L = E/m;
• consider heat losses.

Gas laws:
• control the relevant variables;
• measure pressure/volume/temperature;
• use kelvin;
• plot suitable linearised graphs.

7.22 SOURCES OF ERROR
Temperature experiments suffer from heat loss, thermometer response time, poor insulation and nonuniform temperature.

Gas experiments may suffer from leaks, friction in pistons, calibration errors and temperature changes.

Stress-strain experiments can suffer from extension measurement uncertainty, misalignment and material nonuniformity.

CORE FORMULAE
Q = mcΔT
Q = mL
stress = F/A
strain = ΔL/L
E_Young = stress/strain
F = kx
ΔL = αLΔT
pV = nRT
pV = NkT
p = ρgh
Av = constant
p + 1/2ρv² + ρgh = constant

7.23 SPECIFIC HEAT EXAMPLE
A 2.0 kg material receives 84 kJ and its temperature rises by 20 K.
c = Q/(mΔT)
= 84,000/(2 × 20)
= 2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

7.24 LATENT HEAT EXAMPLE
If 100 kJ melts 0.30 kg of a material at constant temperature:
L = Q/m = 100,000/0.30 ≈ 3.33 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹.

7.25 STRESS AND STRAIN
A wire of cross-sectional area 1.0 × 10⁻6 m² carries a tensile force of 100 N.
Stress = 100/(1.0 × 10⁻6) = 1.0 × 10⁸ Pa.
If original length is 2.0 m and extension is 1.0 mm:
strain = 0.001/2.0 = 5.0 × 10⁻4.
Young modulus = stress/strain = 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa.

7.26 HOOKE'S LAW
If a spring has k = 50 N m⁻¹ and extension is 0.08 m:
F = kx = 4.0 N.
Elastic energy = 1/2kx² = 0.16 J.

7.27 GAS LAW EXAMPLE
A fixed amount of gas occupies 2.0 m³ at 100 kPa and constant temperature. If volume is reduced to 1.0 m³:
p₂ = p₁V₁/V₂ = 200 kPa.
Temperature must remain constant for this calculation.

7.28 KELVIN
A temperature of 27°C is approximately 300 K. In thermodynamic gas calculations, do not substitute 27 for T.

7.29 IDEAL GAS EXAMPLE
For n = 2.0 mol, T = 300 K and V = 0.050 m³:
p = nRT/V
= 2(8.31)(300)/0.050
≈ 9.97 × 10⁴ Pa.

7.30 HYDROSTATIC PRESSURE
At 5 m below the surface of water:
p_gauge = ρgh ≈ 1000(9.81)(5) = 49,050 Pa.
If atmospheric pressure is included, total pressure is atmospheric plus this gauge pressure.

7.31 CONTINUITY
If an incompressible fluid flows from an area of 0.010 m² at 2 m s⁻¹ into an area of 0.005 m²:
A₁v₁ = A₂v₂.
v₂ = 4 m s⁻¹.

7.32 BERNOULLI REASONING
If height is unchanged and fluid speed increases along a streamline in ideal flow, pressure decreases because:
p + 1/2ρv² = constant.
Real flow can include losses, so the ideal equation must be applied with care.

7.33 HEAT TRANSFER COMPARISON
Conduction is strongest in many solids.
Convection requires fluid motion.
Radiation requires no medium.
A vacuum can suppress conduction and convection but not electromagnetic radiation.

7.34 INSULATION DESIGN
A good building envelope may use low-conductivity materials, air gaps, reflective surfaces and controlled ventilation. Moisture must be considered because wet insulating materials can conduct heat more effectively than dry ones.

7.35 EXPERIMENTAL ENERGY LOSSES
In calorimetry, not all electrical input necessarily becomes useful heating of the sample. Heat can enter the container and surroundings. Insulation and a lid reduce losses, while repeated trials improve reliability.
