subject: Physics
topic: 8.0 Modern Physics — Charged Particles, Quantum Physics, Atomic Structure, Radioactivity and Communication
content:
8.0 MODERN PHYSICS
The revised syllabus includes Charged Particles, Quantum Physics, Atomic Structure, Radioactivity and Communication.

8.1 CHARGED PARTICLES
A charged particle in an electric field experiences:
F = qE.

If the electric field is uniform and the particle is free to move:
a = qE/m.

In a magnetic field:
F = Bqv sinθ.

For motion perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field, the magnetic force provides centripetal force:
qvB = mv²/r
so
r = mv/(qB).

The particle follows a circular path if speed is perpendicular to B and no other forces are significant.

Angular frequency:
ω = qB/m
for ideal circular motion.

The magnetic field does no work because force is perpendicular to instantaneous velocity.

8.2 ELECTRON ACCELERATION
An electron accelerated through potential difference V gains kinetic energy:
qV = change in kinetic energy.

For an electron initially at rest:
eV = 1/2mv².

Therefore:
v = √(2eV/m).

Relativistic corrections become necessary at sufficiently high speeds, but use the level of treatment prescribed by the examination context.

8.3 ELECTRON BEAMS AND DEFLECTION
Electric fields can accelerate and deflect charged particles.
Magnetic fields can curve their paths.

Applications include:
mass spectrometry;
particle detectors;
cathode-ray devices;
accelerators.

8.4 QUANTUM PHYSICS
Classical physics cannot fully explain phenomena such as the photoelectric effect.

Quantum ideas describe electromagnetic radiation as energy packets called photons.

Photon energy:
E = hf
and
E = hc/λ.

h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.

Higher frequency means greater photon energy.
Longer wavelength means lower photon energy.

8.5 PHOTOELECTRIC EFFECT
The photoelectric effect is emission of electrons from a material when electromagnetic radiation of sufficient frequency is incident.

Key observations:
• there is a threshold frequency;
• below threshold frequency, increasing intensity alone does not cause emission;
• above threshold, increasing intensity increases photoelectron emission rate;
• maximum photoelectron kinetic energy depends on frequency, not intensity;
• emission is effectively immediate when threshold is exceeded.

Einstein's equation:
hf = φ + K_max.

Work function φ is minimum energy required to liberate an electron.

K_max = eV_s
where V_s is stopping potential.

Threshold frequency:
f₀ = φ/h.

8.6 WAVE-PARTICLE DUALITY
Matter particles also have wave properties.

de Broglie wavelength:
λ = h/p.

For nonrelativistic momentum p = mv:
λ = h/(mv).

The concept helps explain electron diffraction.

8.7 ATOMIC STRUCTURE
An atom contains a small positive nucleus with protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons.

Atomic number Z = number of protons.
Mass/nucleon number A = number of protons + neutrons.

Isotopes have the same proton number but different neutron numbers.

Electrons occupy quantised energy states.

8.8 ELECTRONIC TRANSITIONS
An electron can move between allowed energy levels by absorbing or emitting a photon.

Photon energy:
hf = ΔE.

Emission produces discrete spectral lines because only certain energy differences are allowed.

Absorption spectra occur when photons of particular energies are absorbed.

8.9 ENERGY-LEVEL DIAGRAMS
When an electron drops from a higher level E₂ to lower level E₁:
photon energy = E₂ − E₁ = hf.

The frequency is:
f = (E₂ − E₁)/h.

Shorter wavelength corresponds to larger energy difference.

8.10 NUCLEAR STRUCTURE
The nucleus contains protons and neutrons, collectively called nucleons.

Nuclear forces are strong and short-range and contribute to nuclear stability.

Mass defect is the difference between the mass of separated nucleons and the actual nucleus.

Binding energy:
E = Δmc².

A larger binding energy per nucleon generally corresponds to greater nuclear stability, with the exact stability trend depending on the nucleus.

8.11 RADIOACTIVITY
Radioactivity is spontaneous random decay of unstable nuclei.

Alpha:
helium nucleus, charge +2e, relatively massive, strongly ionising and weakly penetrating.

Beta:
high-energy electron or positron depending on decay type; intermediate penetration and ionisation.

Gamma:
high-frequency electromagnetic radiation; no charge or rest mass; highly penetrating and weakly ionising relative to alpha.

8.12 RADIOACTIVE DECAY LAW
The number of undecayed nuclei follows:
N = N₀e^(−λt).

Activity:
A = λN.

Half-life:
T_1/2 = ln2/λ.

Half-life is the time for the number of undecayed nuclei or activity to fall to half its initial value.

After n half-lives:
N = N₀(1/2)^n.

8.13 ACTIVITY
Activity is the number of decays per second.
Unit: becquerel (Bq).

Background radiation must be considered in measurements.

A typical experiment:
• measure background count rate;
• measure source count rate;
• subtract background appropriately;
• repeat measurements;
• calculate decay relationship.

8.14 HALF-LIFE GRAPH
A graph of activity against time gives an exponential decay curve.

A graph of ln(A) against t should be linear:
ln A = ln A₀ − λt.

Gradient = −λ.

8.15 RADIATION SAFETY
Exposure should be minimised using:
time reduction;
distance increase;
shielding;
appropriate handling;
controlled access.

Alpha, beta and gamma require different shielding because their interactions differ.

8.16 NUCLEAR ENERGY
Fission involves splitting a heavy nucleus into smaller nuclei, releasing energy and often additional neutrons.

A chain reaction can occur when emitted neutrons cause further fissions.

Fusion combines light nuclei and can release large energy because of changes in binding energy.

Nuclear technologies require careful consideration of waste, radiation protection, plant safety and environmental consequences.

8.17 COMMUNICATION
A communication system transfers information from source to destination.

Basic blocks:
source → input transducer → transmitter → communication channel → receiver → output transducer.

Carrier waves can be modulated to carry information.

8.18 BANDWIDTH
Bandwidth is the range of frequencies occupied or supported by a communication channel/system.

Higher bandwidth can support greater information capacity, but requirements depend on modulation and coding.

8.19 NOISE AND SIGNAL QUALITY
Noise is unwanted random disturbance.

Signal-to-noise ratio compares desired signal strength with noise.

Repeaters can restore/regenerate signals along long transmission paths.

Analogue signals may accumulate noise because noise is amplified along with the signal. Digital systems can regenerate ideal logic levels and therefore can maintain quality better over repeated stages, provided the signal remains distinguishable.

8.20 ATTENUATION
Attenuation is reduction in signal strength during transmission.

For power ratios:
number of dB = 10 log₁₀(P₁/P₂).

Attenuation may be expressed in dB per unit length.

Optical fibre offers low attenuation and high bandwidth but requires suitable transmitters, receivers, installation and maintenance.

8.21 COMMUNICATION CHANNELS
Possible channels include:
copper cable;
coaxial cable;
optical fibre;
radio/microwave;
satellite.

Comparison should consider:
bandwidth;
attenuation;
noise;
crosslinking/interference;
security;
repeaters;
regeneration;
cost;
physical installation;
line-of-sight requirements.

8.22 SATELLITES
Geostationary satellites are useful for fixed communication links because they appear stationary relative to the Earth's surface.

Advantages include continuous coverage of a fixed region and stable pointing for ground antennas.

Polar-orbiting satellites are useful for Earth observation because they can cover different regions as Earth rotates beneath the orbit.

8.23 DIGITAL COMMUNICATION
A digital communication chain may include:
sampling → quantisation → encoding → transmission → regeneration → decoding → digital-to-analogue conversion.

Sampling frequency and bit depth affect reproduction quality.

8.24 PRACTICAL COMMUNICATION IDEAS
Students should be able to interpret attenuation graphs, compare channels and explain why repeaters/regenerators are used.

8.25 MODERN PHYSICS EXAM METHOD
For numerical problems:
1. write the governing equation;
2. convert units;
3. substitute known values;
4. show intermediate steps where useful;
5. give the final answer with unit and appropriate significant figures.

For decay problems, identify whether the question asks for N, activity, decay constant or half-life.

For photon problems, identify whether wavelength or frequency is given and use E = hf = hc/λ.

For charged-particle motion, identify whether the particle is parallel or perpendicular to the field.

CORE FORMULAE
F = qE
F = Bqv sinθ
r = mv/(qB)
qV = ΔEk
E_photon = hf = hc/λ
hf = φ + K_max
λ_deBroglie = h/p
E = Δmc²
N = N₀e^(−λt)
A = λN
T_1/2 = ln2/λ
dB = 10 log₁₀(P₁/P₂)

8.26 CHARGED PARTICLE EXAMPLE
An electron enters a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to its velocity. The force is:
F = evB.
This force is perpendicular to velocity and supplies centripetal force:
evB = mv²/r.
Hence r = mv/(eB).

8.27 ELECTRON ACCELERATION
An electron accelerated through 1000 V gains kinetic energy:
ΔE = eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1000
= 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁶ J.
If nonrelativistic treatment is appropriate:
1/2mv² = eV.

8.28 PHOTON EXAMPLE
For wavelength 500 nm:
f = c/λ = 3.00 × 10⁸/(500 × 10⁻9)
= 6.00 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
Photon energy:
E = hf ≈ 3.98 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

8.29 PHOTOELECTRIC EXAMPLE
If a metal has work function 2.0 eV and incident photons have energy 3.5 eV:
maximum kinetic energy = 3.5 − 2.0 = 1.5 eV.
Stopping potential is therefore approximately 1.5 V for singly charged electrons.

8.30 DE BROGLIE EXAMPLE
For a particle of momentum p:
λ = h/p.
Increasing momentum reduces wavelength. Electron diffraction becomes observable because electrons can have sufficiently small de Broglie wavelengths.

8.31 ENERGY LEVEL EXAMPLE
If an electron drops between levels separated by 4.0 eV, the emitted photon has energy 4.0 eV. Its frequency follows f = E/h. Spectral lines therefore provide information about allowed energy differences.

8.32 RADIOACTIVE DECAY EXAMPLE
After three half-lives, remaining fraction:
(1/2)³ = 1/8.
Thus 12.5% remains and 87.5% has decayed, assuming the ideal decay model and no measurement complications.

8.33 DECAY CONSTANT
If half-life is 10 days:
λ = ln2/10 day⁻¹ ≈ 0.0693 day⁻¹.
Convert the time unit if a per-second decay constant is required.

8.34 ACTIVITY
If N = 5.0 × 10¹⁵ nuclei and λ = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹:
A = λN = 1.0 × 10¹⁰ Bq.
The activity decreases as N decreases.

8.35 HALF-LIFE GRAPH
A straight-line graph of ln(activity) against time has gradient −λ. The half-life is then:
T_1/2 = ln2/λ.

8.36 BINDING ENERGY
If a nucleus has a mass defect Δm = 1.0 × 10⁻²⁸ kg:
E = Δmc²
= 1.0 × 10⁻²⁸ × (3.0 × 10⁸)²
= 9.0 × 10⁻¹² J.
Small mass differences can therefore correspond to large nuclear energies.

8.37 RADIATION PENETRATION
Alpha has short range in air and is strongly ionising.
Beta penetrates farther and is moderately ionising.
Gamma is highly penetrating and requires substantial shielding.
Shielding effectiveness depends on radiation type and energy.

8.38 COMMUNICATION ATTENUATION
If transmitted power is 100 W and received power is 1 W:
10 log₁₀(100/1) = 20 dB.
A larger dB value in this expression corresponds to a larger power ratio.

8.39 CHANNEL COMPARISON
Optical fibre generally offers high bandwidth and low attenuation but requires specialised equipment and careful installation. Radio links can cover large areas without physical cables but may experience interference and security issues. Copper can be robust and familiar but has greater attenuation and lower bandwidth than modern optical systems over many applications.

8.40 SATELLITE COMPARISON
Geostationary satellites are advantageous for fixed communication because ground antennas can point at a nearly fixed position. Polar satellites provide repeated coverage of different parts of Earth and are particularly useful for observation.

8.41 MODERN PHYSICS CHECK
Always distinguish:
photon energy from intensity;
activity from number of nuclei;
half-life from decay constant;
mass defect from actual mass;
electric force from magnetic force;
signal attenuation from noise;
sampling rate from bit depth.
source: MoPSE/ZIMSEC Physics Forms 5-6 Syllabus 2024-2030; expanded original study notes

subject: Physics
topic: 9.0 Cross-Syllabus Practical, Mathematical and ZIMSEC Examination Skills
content:
9.0 PRACTICAL AND EXAMINATION SKILLS
The revised Physics syllabus is strongly practical and competency based. The assessment model includes multiple-choice, structured, free-response, practical and school-based project components. Students therefore need more than formula recall.

9.1 SCIENTIFIC METHOD
A strong investigation:
• identifies a question;
• proposes a physical relationship or hypothesis;
• identifies independent, dependent and control variables;
• selects apparatus;
• considers hazards;
• collects measurements;
• repeats readings;
• processes data;
• plots graphs;
• evaluates uncertainty;
• draws a conclusion;
• compares the conclusion with theory;
• suggests improvements.

9.2 VARIABLES
Independent variable: deliberately changed.
Dependent variable: measured response.
Control variables: quantities kept constant to make the test fair.

Example: investigating resistance versus wire length:
independent = length;
dependent = resistance;
controls = material, cross-sectional area and temperature.

9.3 REPEATS
Repeats identify random variation and improve confidence in a mean. If a result is anomalous, investigate before excluding it.

9.4 GRAPH SKILLS
Use the graph to reveal relationships.

If y = mx + c:
gradient = m
intercept = c.

If theory predicts y ∝ x², plot y against x².
If theory predicts y ∝ 1/x, plot y against 1/x.
If theory predicts y ∝ 1/x², plot y against 1/x².

A graph should not be linearised merely because a straight line is easier; the chosen transformation must have physical justification.

9.5 GRADIENT UNITS
The unit of gradient is determined from:
unit of y / unit of x.

Always include units when interpreting physical gradients.

9.6 ERROR BARS
Error bars show uncertainty. A result with large uncertainty should not be treated as equally precise as a result with small uncertainty.

When comparing two measured values, ask whether their uncertainty ranges overlap and whether the difference is physically significant.

9.7 PRACTICAL UNCERTAINTY
Common sources:
instrument resolution;
zero error;
parallax;
reaction time;
environmental fluctuations;
calibration;
heat loss;
friction;
electrical contact resistance;
air resistance.

Improvements should directly target the identified error.

Weak improvement: “use a better instrument.”
Strong improvement: “replace manual stopwatch timing with light gates so reaction-time uncertainty is reduced.”

9.8 MEASUREMENT DESIGN
Choose instrument resolution appropriate to the quantity. Avoid measuring a tiny quantity directly if it can be amplified through a more precise method.

Example: measure a long time for many oscillations and divide by the number of oscillations rather than timing one oscillation.

9.9 UNCERTAINTY REPORTING
If the result is:
x = 2.50 ± 0.05 m,
absolute uncertainty = 0.05 m.
Percentage uncertainty = 0.05/2.50 × 100 = 2%.

For products and quotients, add percentage uncertainties as an appropriate first-order estimate.

9.10 FORMULA USE
Do not substitute numbers before understanding the variables.

Write:
known values;
required quantity;
equation;
substitution;
answer.

Check:
unit;
sign;
magnitude;
direction if vector quantity.

9.11 VECTOR QUESTIONS
Draw the directions. Choose axes. Resolve forces. Use:
ΣFx = ma_x
ΣFy = ma_y.

For equilibrium:
ΣFx = 0
ΣFy = 0.

9.12 FREE-BODY DIAGRAMS
Include only forces acting on the selected object.

Do not include “force of motion”.
Do not include Newton's third-law pair on the same object unless the other body is explicitly being considered.

9.13 ENERGY METHOD
When possible, use conservation of energy to avoid unnecessary force/time calculations.

For an ideal fall:
loss in gravitational potential energy = gain in kinetic energy.

For real systems:
input energy = useful output + dissipated energy + stored energy changes.

9.14 POWER
Power problems often combine energy and time:
P = E/t.
Mechanical motion:
P = Fv.

Electrical:
P = IV.

Do not confuse energy with power.

9.15 UNITS CHECK
Useful checks:
force N = kg m s⁻²
energy J = N m
power W = J s⁻¹
charge C = A s
potential difference V = J C⁻¹
resistance Ω = V A⁻¹.

Dimensional consistency can reveal algebraic mistakes.

9.16 COMMAND WORDS
Define: precise meaning.
State: concise fact.
Describe: features or sequence.
Explain: give reasons/physics.
Calculate: show working and answer.
Determine: obtain a value from given information/data.
Deduce: derive from supplied information or known relationships.
Suggest: reasonable proposal supported by physics.
Compare: similarities and differences.
Discuss: balanced, developed consideration.
Evaluate: judge using evidence/criteria.

9.18 SCHOOL-BASED PROJECT
The revised assessment framework includes school-based project work. A strong project moves from:
problem identification → investigation → possible solutions → selection → refinement → presentation → evaluation/recommendations.

The project should solve a genuine problem and show evidence rather than simply describe an idea.

9.19 COMMON PHYSICS MISTAKES
• using centimetres instead of metres;
• using Celsius instead of kelvin in gas laws;
• mixing scalar and vector quantities;
• forgetting the square on inverse-square relationships;
• using g with the wrong sign;
• confusing mass and weight;
• confusing energy and power;
• confusing emf and terminal potential difference;
• using RMS as if it were peak voltage;
• confusing frequency with angular frequency;
• forgetting that magnetic force is perpendicular to velocity;
• using an equation outside its assumptions;
• reporting excessive significant figures;
• ignoring uncertainty;
• drawing graphs without units;
• treating every discrepancy as random error.

9.20 FORMULA SHEET HABITS
Do not rely on memorising isolated equations. Understand relationships:
Newtonian mechanics connects F, m and a.
Energy connects force, displacement, speed and height.
Circular motion connects v, r, ω and force.
Fields connect force with source properties and distance.
Electric circuits connect V, I, R and power.
Waves connect v, f and λ.
Quantum physics connects E, f and λ.
Radioactivity connects activity, number of nuclei and decay constant.

9.21 FINAL REVISION STRATEGY
For each topic:
1. learn definitions;
2. understand the physical model;
3. derive important equations;
4. practise substitution;
5. practise multi-step problems;
6. practise graph/data questions;
7. practise practical questions;
8. explain concepts without equations;
9. review common mistakes;
10. attempt timed ZIMSEC-style questions.

The highest-quality preparation combines conceptual understanding, calculation fluency, practical reasoning and communication.
